lessons.title: Moving Average Reversion and the Buy the Dip Trap

children.text: "Buy the dip" is probably India's most repeated piece of market wisdom, on FinTwit, in WhatsApp trading groups, in every comment section under a red candle. It is also, whether the person saying it realizes it or not, a mean reversion strategy: buy when the price falls below its moving average, on the assumption it reverts back up to it. Sometimes that is exactly what happens. Sometimes it is catching a falling knife on the way to a permanently lower price, the exact trap Chapter 1's Alpha Industries and Yes Bank examples warned about. This lesson gives you one concrete rule for telling the two apart before your capital finds out the hard way.

body.text: A moving-average reversion strategy buys a price dip below its own average expecting it to revert back up to that average. The strategy is only statistically sound when the moving average itself is a stable, roughly flat target. When the average is sliding in the same direction as the price, the target you are betting on reversion toward is itself falling away from you.

children.text: Two Different Uses of a Moving Average
Moving averages get used for two genuinely different, sometimes contradictory, purposes, and mixing them up is a common source of confusion.

body.caption: Two different theses, both built from moving averages

cells: Golden Cross / Death Cross (50-day MA crossing 200-day MA)
The direction the moving averages themselves are heading
Momentum: a trend, once confirmed, tends to continue
Buy the dip (price vs its own MA)
How far price has strayed from a rolling average
Mean reversion: a stretched deviation tends to correct

body.text: These two techniques can disagree about the same stock at the same time, and that is not a contradiction. A stock can be in a confirmed long-term uptrend (a bullish golden cross, a case for momentum) while also being short-term overbought relative to its own 20-day average (a case for a short-term reversion trade against that trend). They are answering different questions over different time frames. This lesson is only about the second one.

children.text: Stripped of sentiment, a buy-the-dip rule is usually some version of this: buy when the price falls more than X percent below its N-day moving average, and exit when it reverts back to that average. A common version uses a 50-day moving average and an 8 percent threshold. That is a perfectly legitimate mean reversion rule. Whether it makes money depends entirely on one thing this simple description leaves out.
When It Works: A Flat, Range-Bound Mean

Consider a stock whose 50-day moving average has sat close to ₹300 for months, drifting only slightly as the business ticks along without major news. A short-term dip to ₹270, about 10 percent below that average, is a textbook case: the average is a stable, meaningful target, and there is a real business reason to expect the price to work its way back toward it over the following weeks, exactly the mechanism behind Chapter 1's Alpha Industries recovery.
The Trap: A Falling Mean Chasing the Price Down

markDefs.definition: A brief, partial price recovery during an overall structural decline, which looks like a reversion setting up but is quickly followed by the decline resuming.

children.text: Now consider a stock in genuine, ongoing trouble, the same shape of story as DHFL or Jet Airways from Chapter 1. Three months ago its 50-day moving average also sat near ₹300. Since then the price has been sliding steadily on real, worsening news, and the moving average has been sliding right along with it, down to ₹220 today. A trader spots the price at ₹195, about 11 percent below today's average, and buys the dip, expecting reversion toward ₹220. The problem is that ₹220 was never a stable target. It was already a falling average chasing a falling price. Over the following weeks the price keeps sliding to ₹150, punctuated by a couple of sharp, brief rallies, a

, that look enough like the start of a reversion to draw in a second round of dip buyers, while the moving average itself keeps falling to meet the price rather than the other way around. The moving goalpost is the trap: the statistical setup looked identical to the healthy case, a price stretched below its average, but the average itself was not the fixed reference point the strategy assumes it to be.

body.title: Flat mean vs falling mean: same 'dip', opposite outcomes (illustrative)

body.text: Look at Stock B's brief rally around week 5, from ₹230 back up to ₹240. To a dip buyer, that would have looked like the reversion working. It was a dead cat bounce inside a decline that resumed the following week. The tell was never in the bounce itself. It was in the moving average's own downward slope the whole time.

children.text: The practical fix is to measure the moving average's own slope before trusting it as a reversion target, and skip the trade when that slope is too steep in either direction. A simple version compares today's moving average to its value 20 trading days ago, as a percentage change. Stock A's 50-day MA barely moved over that stretch. Stock B's fell hard. That single number would have flagged Stock B's "dip" as untrustworthy before a single rupee was risked.

body.code:
import pandas as pd

window = 50
dip_threshold = -0.08       # buy when price is 8% or more below the MA
slope_lookback = 20
max_slope = 0.03            # skip the trade if the MA moved more than 3%
                             # over the slope_lookback window, either direction

ma = close.rolling(window).mean()
dip_pct = (close - ma) / ma
ma_slope = ma.pct_change(slope_lookback)

buy_the_dip = (dip_pct < dip_threshold) & (ma_slope.abs() < max_slope)

print(pd.DataFrame({"dip_pct": dip_pct, "ma_slope": ma_slope, "buy_signal": buy_the_dip}).tail())
body.caption: A buy-the-dip rule with a slope filter: only treat a dip below the moving average as a reversion candidate when that average itself is roughly flat.

body.title: Measure the moving average's slope
body.prompt: A stock's 50-day moving average was ₹450 twenty trading days ago and is ₹417 today. What is the 20-day percentage change in the moving average?
body.explanation: (417 - 450) / 450 = -33 / 450 = -0.0733, or -7.33%. With a max_slope filter of 3%, a 7.33% move in the average over just 20 days would flag this stock's moving average as unreliable as a flat reversion target, exactly the falling-mean trap.

body.title: Genuine setup or moving goalpost?
body.question: Two stocks are both trading 9% below their 50-day moving average today. Stock P's 50-day MA has moved less than 1% over the last 20 trading days. Stock Q's 50-day MA has fallen 12% over the last 20 trading days. Which is the more trustworthy mean reversion candidate?
options: Stock Q, because a falling average means the reversion target is closer to the current price
Stock P, because its flat moving average is a genuinely stable target, while Stock Q's falling average is a moving goalpost
Both are equally trustworthy since the dip percentage is identical
Neither can be evaluated without knowing the exact rupee prices involved
body.explanation: The size of the dip below the moving average tells you nothing on its own. Stock P's flat moving average has been a stable reference point for weeks, making its 9% dip a plausible reversion setup. Stock Q's moving average has fallen 12% in the same stretch, meaning the 'target' the reversion trade is betting on is itself sliding away, the exact falling-mean trap this lesson covers.

cards.definition: A mean reversion rule that buys a price after it falls a set percentage below its own moving average, expecting it to revert back toward that average.

A momentum-based signal from a shorter moving average crossing above (golden) or below (death) a longer one, a different technique from price-vs-MA reversion, sometimes giving contradictory signals over different time frames.
A brief, partial price recovery during an overall structural decline that resembles the start of a reversion but is quickly followed by the decline resuming.
A check on how much a moving average has itself moved over a recent window, used to skip buy-the-dip trades where the reversion target is not stable.

points: A buy-the-dip strategy is a mean reversion rule that buys a price stretched below its moving average, expecting it to revert back toward that average.
Golden cross and death cross signals are a different, momentum-based use of moving averages and can validly disagree with a short-term reversion signal on the same stock.

The strategy only works when the moving average itself is a stable target. When the average is sliding in the same direction as the price, the 'reversion' target is itself moving away, the falling-mean trap.
A dead cat bounce can look identical to a genuine reversion in progress. The moving average's own slope, not the bounce itself, is what actually distinguishes the two.
A simple slope filter, skipping dips where the moving average has moved more than a small percentage over a recent window, is a concrete, testable fix Chapter 7 builds on directly.
